procedural_history.originating_court: Principal Consumer Disputes Redressal for Bangalore Urban District, at Bangalore (‘District Forum’)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 10.03.2021 of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi (NCDRC)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The OP filed WP No.22568/2012 with 9 other connected writ petitions against the order of the Additional Registrar. The Complainant also filed WP No.17045/2014 with 9 other connected writ petitions questioning the finding with regards to the maintainability under the Chit Funds Act. On 16.11.2015, the High Court directed the complainant to approach the Consumer Forum and held that said cases were not maintainable under the Chit Funds Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (‘OP’/‘service provider’) challenged the order of the NCDRC after being unsuccessful before the District Forum and the State Forum. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the consumer complaint was not maintainable on the ground that the service obtained by the complainant was for a commercial purpose.

facts: The service provider (Opposite Party or OP) raised a preliminary objection that the consumer complaint was not maintainable.

The OP's argument was that the service was obtained by the complainant for a 'commercial purpose', which would exclude them from the definition of a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
The OP relied on two points to support its claim: a statement in the complaint about an 'understanding... to promote chit business' and the findings of an internal audit.
The lower forums had not properly decided this specific issue; the District Forum had incorrectly focused on whether the complainant was a 'person' rather than on the purpose of the service.
law: The Consumer Protection Act is a consumer-friendly and beneficial legislation.
The onus (burden of proof) to prove that a service was obtained for a commercial purpose lies entirely on the service provider who makes that claim.
A negative burden cannot be placed on the complainant to prove that the service was *not* for a commercial purpose.
The standard of proof for the service provider is a 'preponderance of probabilities'.

Only if the service provider successfully proves the service was for a commercial purpose does the onus shift to the complainant to prove their case falls under the exception (i.e., that the service was exclusively for earning a livelihood by means of self-employment).
A plea made without any supporting proof is not considered evidence in the eyes of the law.
application: The Court found that the OP had merely pleaded in its written version that the service was for a commercial purpose.
The OP failed to lead any evidence to 'probabilise its case other than merely restating its claim on affidavit'.
Since the OP did not discharge its initial onus of proving the service was for a commercial purpose, the burden of proof never shifted to the complainant.
Therefore, the OP's argument that the complainant had failed to plead or prove the 'livelihood by self-employment' exception was irrelevant, as that stage of the inquiry was never reached.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the service provider's argument and held that the complaint was maintainable. The Court reasoned that the service provider had the burden to prove the service was for a commercial purpose and had completely failed to provide any evidence to support its claim, rendering the objection baseless.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a deficiency in service by the Opposite Party.

facts: The complainant alleged deficiency in service due to the illegal termination of a chit fund business and the subsequent non-refund of the subscription amount.
The District Forum examined the case on its merits and found that there was a deficiency in service.
The State Forum, on appeal, agreed with the District Forum's conclusion that there was a deficiency in service.
The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) also concurred with the findings of the two lower forums on the merits of the issue.
law: The Supreme Court generally does not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by multiple lower forums, especially when three forums have reached the same conclusion on the merits of an issue.
application: The Supreme Court observed that three separate forums (District Forum, State Forum, and NCDRC) had all previously examined the evidence and the merits of the case.
All three of these forums had concurred in their finding that a deficiency of service by the Opposite Party had been proven.
Given this consistent finding across the lower forums, the Supreme Court decided it was not necessary for it to re-address or re-evaluate the merits of the deficiency of service claim.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that there was a deficiency in service by the Opposite Party because three lower forums had already concurrently arrived at that same conclusion, and the Court saw no reason to interfere with this consistent finding.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the consumer complaint was not maintainable on the ground that the service obtained by the complainant was for a commercial purpose.
appellant_arguments: The consumer complaint was not maintainable because the service was obtained for a commercial purpose.
respondent_arguments: The appellant failed to provide any evidence to support its claim that the service was for a commercial purpose, offering only a restatement of the claim on an affidavit.
A plea without proof is not considered evidence in the eyes of the law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a deficiency in service by the Opposite Party.
appellant_arguments: There was no deficiency in service. (Inferred from their appeal against the concurrent findings of the District and State Forums).
respondent_arguments: The appellant was deficient in service by failing to pay an amount as directed by an award from the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies, which was upheld on appeal.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A plea without proof and proof without plea is no evidence in the eyes of law.
obiter: The court will not address the merits of an issue when three lower forums have concurred in their findings.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The onus to prove that a service was obtained for a commercial purpose rests on the service provider. In this case, the service provider failed to discharge this onus, as it provided no evidence to support its claim other than merely restating it on an affidavit. A plea without proof is not considered evidence in the eyes of the law, and therefore the consumer complaint was maintainable.
legal_tests_applied: The standard of proof for determining if a service was for a 'commercial purpose' is the 'preponderance of probabilities'.

A two-step burden-shifting framework applies: First, the service provider bears the onus of proving the service was for a commercial purpose. Second, if and only if the service provider discharges this onus, the burden then shifts to the complainant to show that the service was obtained exclusively for earning a livelihood by means of self-employment.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant, as the service provider, bore the onus of proving that the service was obtained for a commercial purpose, but failed to discharge it.
The appellant led no evidence to probabilise its case, offering only a restatement of its claim on an affidavit.
The court applied the principle that a 'plea without proof and proof without plea is no evidence in the eyes of law.'

The appellant's argument that the complainant failed to prove the service was for earning a livelihood was premature, as the burden to prove that only arises after the service provider first proves the existence of a commercial purpose.
why_respondent_won: The onus of proof correctly rested on the service provider (appellant) to establish that the service was for a commercial purpose.

Since the service provider failed to discharge its initial onus, the burden of proof never shifted to the complainant (respondent) to prove that the service fell within the 'livelihood by means of self-employment' exception.
policy_considerations: The Consumer Protection Act is a consumer-friendly and beneficial legislation intended to address the grievances of consumers.
A negative burden cannot be placed on the complainant to show that the service they availed was not for a commercial purpose.
